newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK economy grows estimated 2.3 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK economy grows estimated 2.3 pct in 1996.

text.p: The British economy grew by a stately 0.8 percent in the final three months of 1996 and by an estimated 2.3 percent in the year as a whole, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Monday.
The figures, which are preliminary, suggested the economy was growing steadily but showed little sign of overheating.

Conservative finance minister Kenneth Clarke said the economy was going "from strength and strength" and economists said the figures improved his chances of avoiding a politically embarrassing rise in interest rates before the looming election.
The ONS said gross domestic product (GDP) grew a preliminary 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter from the third and was up 2.6 percent compared with the fourth quarter of 1995.
Higher output from the energy industry was largely responsible for the growth seen in the fourth quarter as unusually cold weather boosted demand for gas and electricity.
Service sector output grew slightly while agricultural output fell. Excluding oil and gas production, the ONS said GDP rose 0.7 percent on the quarter.
It estimated that the British economy grew by 2.3 percent over 1996 as a whole compared with 1.8 percent in 1995.
"The latest data suggest the economy ended last year and started this year with less momentum than expected," said Robert Barrie, UK economist at BZW.
Economists said the figures would help Clarke to resist pressure from Bank of England Governor Eddie George to raise official interest rates from the present six percent.

George has been pressing for higher rates because he believes inflation will head higher again in the next 18 months, but Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, has so far refused to budge.
Monday's GDP figures could be a key factor when the two men meet for their monthly monetary policy meeting next week.

"It leaves the interest rate decision on February 5 a bit more in balance than if it had come in as we expected," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "But on balance, I think Clarke will probably leave rates unchanged."
Clarke is keen to avoid raising interest rates in the next few months as this would mean higher mortgage payments for millions of home-owners with variable-rate loans.
The government must hold an election by May and the opposition Labour Party has a strong lead in opinion polls.
Recent figures suggest Clarke may be able to hold fire.

A shock 0.8 percent fall in retail sales in December suggested a much heralded consumer-led boom has still failed to take off. Many of Britain's large high street groups have complained of disappointing Christmas sales.
Manufacturing output also fell unexpectedly in December.

Clarke has also argued that the strength of the pound -- up more than 13 percent against major currencies since last August -- reduces the need to tighten monetary policy as it cuts import prices and puts a brake on Britain's struggling manufacturers.

The last time Clarke raised base rates, by a quarter-point to six percent on October 30, he said the fact that GDP had accelerated and was likely to continue doing so was "very relevant to the decision on interest rates."
Economists expect the Bank of England to maintain its campaign for higher rates.

"Eddie George will no doubt continue to press for further policy tightening, arguing that buoyancy in the domestic economy will continue unabated by sterling's strength," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
